query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor addition (~5 atomic%) of vanadium (V) into the equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy will improve its room‐temperature ductility and irradiation resistance while maintaining its high‐temperature mechanical performance and BCC structural stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW with excellent high-temperature strength but poor room-temperature ductility and uncertain experimental irradiation tolerance.
generation.intervention: Alloying NbMoTaW with approximately 5 at.% vanadium (V) to form a modified BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests at room temperature (to assess ductility) and at high temperatures (up to 1600 °C) for strength retention; irradiation conditions mimicking helium and heavy-ion exposure representative of reactor environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of the predominant BCC lattice with increased lattice distortion and the creation of additional defect sink sites.
generation.mechanism: The added V is expected to subtly modify the lattice distortion, lowering dislocation motion barriers at room temperature to improve ductility. In parallel, the enhanced lattice distortion and defect sinks are anticipated to promote recombination of irradiation-induced defects (such as vacancies and helium bubbles), thereby mitigating blistering and amorphization without significantly altering the high-temperature phase stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the V-alloyed variant should exhibit higher room-temperature ductility (evidenced by higher elongation and lower yield stress) and reduced irradiation damage (fewer/lower-size helium bubbles and less defect accumulation), while still maintaining comparable high-temperature strength and structural stability.
generation.baseline: Untreated equal-atomic NbMoTaW that exhibits excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and BCC stability but poor ductility and unverified irradiation tolerance.
generation.boundary: Performance improvements are expected under temperatures from room temperature to 1600 °C and under irradiation conditions simulating helium and heavy-ion exposures as found in nuclear reactor environments.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of ductility and irradiation resistance improvement is uncertain and depends critically on the precise V concentration and processing conditions. There is also a risk that inappropriate doping may lead to secondary phase formation, potentially compromising high-temperature properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of refractory alloys: pure NbMoTaW and NbMoTaW alloyed with ~5 at.% V. Conduct tensile tests at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (up to 1600 °C) to compare ductility and high-temperature strength. Then, expose both alloys to controlled irradiation conditions using helium ions and a heavy ion beam to simulate nuclear environments. Microstructural changes should be characterized using TEM and XRD.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile properties (yield strength, elongation to fracture)
Irradiation-induced defect density and helium bubble size/distribution (TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the V-alloyed alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility or irradiation resistance compared to pure NbMoTaW, or if it exhibits compromised high-temperature strength or the formation of new deleterious phases.

Most similar research was concerned with microstrain and lattice parameter changes in HEAs. In HEAs and steels including 316L and 304H, helium irradiation usually leads to lattice expansion [,]. Helium irradiation led to lattice expansion in VCrFeMn []. However, in HEAs such as non-equiatomic Ti2ZrHfV0.5Mo0.2, lattice parameters can be reduced by helium ion irradiation due to higher lattice distortion []. Lattice expansion and microstrain can also be increased by irradiation with non-heavy ions such as Ni and C. Irradiation by Ni ions resulted in lattice expansion in FeCoNiCr and FeCoNiCrMn []. cited_evidence.text: The elemental content and main phases of CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were preserved despite successive irradiation with krypton (280 keV, 5 × 1015 cm−2) and helium (40 keV, 2 × 1017 cm−2) ions; new phases did not emerge, but several blisters formed on the surface of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA, although with a smaller average size than in Ni. Fewer large blisters formed in the HEA probably because of lattice distortion, low defect mobility and weakened helium bubble formation [,]. It can be seen that Kr irradiation enhances the surface damage leading to blister formation at room temperature compared to He-only irradiation, which was carried out in []. Analysis of the results of the study of macrostresses and density of dislocations in HEAs showed that the main changes obtained as a result of sample irradiation are probably associated with the formation, interaction and migration of radiation-induced defects and their clusters, which modified stresses in the alloys.
